what.title: What is a Transformer?
what.body: A Transformer is a sequence model built around attention. Instead of reading text strictly left-to-right, it lets tokens compare with other tokens and build richer context-aware representations.

flow.title: High-level LLM flow
flow.body: A language model turns raw text into a chain of representations, then predicts what token is likely to come next.

architecture.title: Encoder / Decoder architecture
architecture.body: Classic Transformers include encoders and decoders. Modern chat LLMs often use decoder-only stacks, but the same attention-centered building blocks remain central.

attention.title: Self-attention and multi-head attention
attention.body: Attention is the routing mechanism: each token decides how strongly it should listen to other tokens. Multi-head attention repeats this through several learned views.

components.title: Key Transformer components
components.body: The full block is a compact rhythm: attention, residual connection, normalization, feed forward network, residual connection, normalization.

interactive.title: Try it: Transformer demo
interactive.body: Run a simulated forward pass. The goal is visualization and intuition, so the attention weights are approximate rather than model-internal measurements.

glossary.title: Glossary
glossary.body: A few compact definitions for the terms that appear across Transformer papers, model cards, and LLM tooling.

components.title: Self-Attention
components.body: Scores token-to-token relationships and blends the most useful context.

components.title: Multi-Head Attention
components.body: Runs several attention patterns in parallel, then merges them.

components.title: Positional Encoding
components.body: Adds order information so the model knows where tokens sit.

components.title: Feed Forward Network
components.body: Transforms each contextual token vector through learned nonlinear layers.

components.title: Add & Norm
components.body: Stabilizes deep stacks with residual paths and normalization.

components.title: Token Prediction
components.body: Turns final vectors into vocabulary probabilities.

components.title: Embeddings
components.body: Represent each token as a dense vector the network can compute with.

components.title: Transformer Layers
components.body: Repeat attention, residual, normalization, and feed forward blocks.

header.title: Quantization Playground
header.description: Simulate how lower numerical precision changes sample weights, model memory, and approximation error.

cards.title: Precision cards
cards.description: Lower bit widths save memory but provide fewer representable values.

guide.title: Fewer bits, smaller model
guide.body: Quantization reduces the number of bits used to store model weights. Compact weights need less RAM or VRAM, but rounding them to fewer values introduces approximation error.
bullets: FP16 and INT8 often preserve more detail while reducing memory compared with FP32.
Q4, Q5, and Q8 variants are common when running local LLMs through GGUF, llama.cpp, or Ollama.
Real quantizers may operate per tensor, channel, or block and store additional scales and zero points.
Smaller files do not guarantee identical model quality or faster inference on every device.
guide.disclaimer: {{disclaimer}} This playground does not create or modify a real model file. The compression animation is a visual learning aid; production quantization uses tools and formats such as GGUF, llama.cpp, GPTQ, AWQ, bitsandbytes, and Ollama-compatible model files.

ragWorkbench.sampleDocument:
React Query is a server state management library for React applications. It handles caching, background refetching, retries, loading states, and synchronization between the UI and remote data.

Embeddings are numerical representations of meaning. A sentence, document, or query can be transformed into a vector so similar ideas stay close together in vector space.

Retrieval augmented generation, also called RAG, connects search with language generation. The system splits a document into chunks, embeds those chunks, retrieves the most relevant pieces for a user question, and injects them into the model prompt.

Chunking matters because language models have limited context windows. If chunks are too large, retrieval becomes noisy. If chunks are too small, important explanations can be broken apart.

Overlap repeats a small amount of text between neighboring chunks. It helps preserve context when a paragraph or idea crosses a chunk boundary.

Top-k retrieval means selecting the k most relevant chunks for a query. A low k can miss useful evidence, while a high k can add distracting context.

The final generation step should answer using the retrieved chunks and cite the source chunks. This makes the answer easier to inspect and reduces unsupported claims.

defaults.question: Why do chunking and overlap matter in RAG?

header.description: Split a source into chunks, preserve context with overlap, retrieve top-k evidence, and inspect the prompt that would be sent to an LLM.
